utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you cal the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I will now ask the Prosecution for the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Mrs. Tecla Benjamin and Ekkehard Withopf, together with Mrs. Kimberly Fleming, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And could we have the appearances for the Defence. The team hasn't changed, but since it's traditional to have the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic; Stephane Bourgon is co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic is the legal assistant, and we are representing General Hadzihasanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. Mr. Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, our legal assistant, representing Mr. Kupreskic -- Mr. Kubura.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Antonetti, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the accused. As far as I have understood, we have two witnesses for today. And if the examination doesn't take too long, we might be able to conclude the hearing of these two witnesses today. And as a result, there would be no hearing tomorrow, which would save resources. So if we fail to conclude the examination of the two witnesses today, we shall continue tomorrow. If we conclude with the hearing of these two witnesses, there will be no hearing tomorrow, and this will allow both parties to continue with their work. If there are no other issues to raise or comments to make, I'm going to ask the usher to bring the new witness in the courtroom, if no protective measures have been requested. We will, therefore, be in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. Could you tell me whether you can hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have been called as a witness for the Prosecution, and the Prosecution will put a series of questions to you and then you will also be cross-examined by the Defence. But first of all, could you please give me your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ivan Tvrtkovic. I was born on the 5th of September, 1940, in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What is your address?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I live in Zagreb, Miramarska 38, Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a mining engineer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The usher will show you a text that you should read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. As I have said, you will now be asked some questions by the Prosecution, who are to your right, and you will then be examined by the Defence, who are to your left. If necessary, the Judges who are before you will also ask you some questions. We would like to point out that we are not familiar with your testimony. We don't know what you're going to say. We don't know the context within which you have been called to testify here. So the responses that you provide will inform the Trial Chamber of the facts that you are a witness of, either an eyewitness or you heard things. You will -- we will ask you not to interpret facts that you did not witness directly. You have to testify with regard to facts that took place over ten years ago, but facts that you yourself witnessed. If there are any questions that you do not understand, you can ask the person who has put you the question to rephrase the question. Take your time to respond to the questions that you are asked. And to the extent that it is possible, could you fully answer the questions and not answer them just by saying yes or no. Having mentioned this, the Prosecution may now take the floor to conduct its examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. President. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon. Could you please state for the Trial Chamber the municipality in which you remember born.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in the municipality of Kakanj in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, kindly could you state for the Trial Chamber the ethnic breakdown of this village.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: To the extent that I followed the situation, I think that there were about 45 or 46 -- I think about 45 or 46 per cent of the population was Muslim and about 27 or 28 per cent of the population were Croats; 12 or 13 per cent were Serbs; and then there were others, those who declared themselves to be Yugoslavs or members of other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Trial Chamber, Witness, can you please describe the relationship which existed between the villagers of your village.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I must say that in the municipality in which I lived we lived in harmony, in fact. It was a mining municipality. It was also somewhat international in character. Mining brings people together, because they work together underground and they simply have to demonstrate solidarity and help each other. As far as the villagers themselves are concerned, there were villages next to each other, both Serb and Muslim and Croat villages. I don't recall there have been conflicts of any kind or judicial proceedings, court proceedings. I don't remember anything of that kind. But in the course of my work, as far as that matter is concerned, there was never even a trace of hatred. No one ever said anything or commented or said that I was doing one thing or another thing for certain reasons. So I can say that that was an issue that was not even considered to be a problem. It wasn't even thought about.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, did you at any time serve in the national service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In 1963, in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And upon completion of your national service, could you kindly tell the Chamber what you did.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: When I completed my military service, I went to Zagreb, and I graduated from the university. Before -- when I went to the army, I hadn't yet graduated. I returned. I graduated. And then I immediately went to Kakanj. I had a grant from the Kakanj mine, and I had to pay it back. I had to work to pay back the grant for as long as it took me to study. My parents, my grandparents lived in that place, and it was my duty to give back what I had been given. So on the 22nd of November, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. started working in the Kakanj mine, 1992, and I worked there continually --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: -- until the end, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, would you say that you were actively involved in your local community?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in a certain sense, yes. I was involved in sport. I was involved in gymnastics, et cetera. When I grew a little older, then I became a manager of sports organisations. I was one of the founders of the volleyball club in Kakanj. We were very successful. We were in the second league in the former Yugoslavia, and I was the president of the volleyball team of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was a member of the presidency of the volleyball association of Yugoslavia and the director of the club, a member of when it was founded, and for the last four years I was its director too. So much of my free time was spent in the field of sports.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you say then, Witness, that you were a well-known person in the municipality of Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'd have to say so. It's perhaps a matter of interest, but I was the first and for a long time the first mining engineer who came from the town itself, who was born in the town itself. I'm not -- I don't remember whether there were any other people like me. My roots are there, and everyone knew me because of my involvement in sports and in management and my professional involvement. I think that everyone knew me, but it's difficult to speak about oneself.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You indicated to the Trial Chamber that you commenced employment in November of 1969. Prior to the commencement of June 1993, did you observe in the environment of your workplace whether any command post of any sort was set up in your area?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: In the Kakanj mine, no, I didn't notice a command post. No such orders had been issued. No such post had been established, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that in fact in and around the mines, that headquarters for the different armies were stationed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that process, the process of forming the armies, followed its own course. I couldn't exactly tell you when that took place, but I know that we in the mine, on the basis of requests from the BH Army and the HVO, we would provide them with certain facilities for their use. We would provide certain equipment for their use, some machines. The general director had the authority to allow these two formations to use certain features, equipment, and other items, other facilities that they needed for accommodation and for the purpose of conducting their operations. This had to do with the equipment that the mine disposed of.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I now wish you to cast your mind back particularly to the period commencing June 1993 and tell the Trial Chamber at the commencement of June 1993 how you felt living and working in the municipality of Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: The overall situation in Yugoslavia at the time was reflected directly or indirectly in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also in Kakanj. And as coal producers, the Kakanj mine produced about 2 million tons of coal at the time; or, in fact, in its best years, that was its production capacity. But at that time, we were providing a sufficient amount of coal for the Kakanj powerplant, because we knew it was essential for it to be operational. So most of the activity - since I was in -- I was part of the management of the mine - all of our activities had to do with providing the basic material and everything that was necessary for the work of the mine. I think that all the other activities, personal, social, et cetera, were relegated to the background, whereas the management activities were of greatest importance. Through international organisations we asked -- we asked international organisations to assist us, and we were provided with equipment, et cetera. We'd then exchange it, et cetera, et cetera. So we did everything we could so ensure that the work of the mine continued smoothly. We had to make sure that we had enough material and food and so on. So together with our management, the general director at the time - who was a very versatile man and wanted the mine to work continually - we took care of this, and in fact we didn't have the possibility of carrying out any other activities. So these are the activities we were concerned with, and we weren't perhaps even able to have a wider view of what was happening around us. At least, I wasn't in a position to have such a view.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Trial Chamber, Witness, could you assist us as to the commencement of June 1993 -- or from the commencement of June 1993, what you thought or how you thought, what kind of relationship existed between the villagers themselves then.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is how I would put it, as briefly as possible: There were individual conflicts between Muslims and -- between Muslims themselves and between Croats themselves. I know about conflicts between Croats. There were even dead people. But as far as conflicts between Muslims and Croats are concerned, I'm not aware of any such conflicts. I have to emphasise that I'm not aware of any such conflicts. Everyone tried to avoid insulting others or to harming others. And perhaps this is interesting, but I knew and I heard that elsewhere such things had happened, but in our community I'm not aware of any such incidents. I know about conflicts that concerned Croats themselves. People's interests were at stake, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Kindly please state, Witness, for the Trial Chamber, your duties as they were at the beginning of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the management committee for development and investment -- or rather, director of investment concerned with the development of the mine. There were four members, and the general director. I was one of the four members of the management committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: As a consequence of your duties, were you called upon at times to attend meetings?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I sometimes attended some meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 12th of June specifically, you reported to duty, as customary.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in fact, the 12th was a Saturday, and at that time, during that period of time, Saturday and Sunday just didn't mean anything. We worked every day. So yes, one could say that I went to work on that day, just as I had done every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And whilst at work, did you receive any instructions from anyone?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean exactly. I can only say what happened when I arrived at work.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. When you arrived at work, did you have any meetings to attend to, on the 12th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had meetings of the managing board every morning, and at those meetings we would examine the current situation, in terms of production and providing coal to the powerplant. So I knew that it was my duty to turn up at work, and that's how I turned up at work that morning too and went to the office, to the general director's office, which is where we held the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you receive any specific instructions to go anywhere on that day?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived there, the general director and the director for legal matters were standing by the table. They seemed fairly downcast. I think I even noticed tears in their eyes. They told me that Stjepan Mijac, Jozo Pavlovic, and myself were being looked for by the BH military police. They said that they wanted to speak to me, the BH Army military police. I said that I had nothing against that. The director said that he would provide a car immediately to have us driven to the command where we would have a discussion. He said it wasn't convenient, it wouldn't be good for the police to come looking for us there again. The director provided the car and a driver. We got into the car, and we went to the command to have a discussion there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: At the location where this discussion was to have taken place, would you be able to tell the Trial Chamber if you observed anything that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was unusual in any way on the outside of the compound.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: In the mine itself or, rather, in the compound where we entered and where the command was, was also the compound of the Kakanj mine previously, as I said to begin with. So the mine provided that facility to the BH Army to use for its needs. When we got there, there was a lot of movement on the part of the soldiers. You could hear shooting, because the conflicts had already started and they were ongoing. You could hear explosions coming from afar and different types of weapons being used. So that went on for a day or two. So we had already become accustomed to hearing that kind of noise. The army entered. Soldiers would come and go. Quite simply -- how shall I put it? There was a lot of lively activity going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, for how long were you engaged in this discussion? What period of time were you engaged in this discussion?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there for about 40 minutes perhaps. But there wasn't any discussion. There was no questioning, no interrogation of any kind, no giving of statements. All we did was to sit down and talk to the people who we otherwise knew, and nobody said that we were actually being questioned, nor were we asked for a statement of any kind. So that's how the 40 or 50 minutes went by, one hour at the most.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Kindly tell the Trial Chamber what happened next at the end of the 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: After 40 minutes, people would be coming in and leaving, because it was a room with several doors. So people would be passing by. They didn't stay there for any length of time. And at one particular point Jasko turned up. I learnt that his name was Jasko later on, but I did know the man otherwise. And the commander, I think his name was Hodzic or Hadzic, and he said that we were to go with Jasko. There was myself and also Pero Pavlovic and Stjepan Mijac, the three of us. And the three of us were told to follow Jasko, to go with him. And that's what we did, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And did you go with Jasko?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you know Jasko?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Jasko was a young man from town. Yes, I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber - if you know, that is - the ethnic background of Jasko.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Jasko was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, you indicated to the Trial Chamber that you followed Jasko. Could you tell us: Followed Jasko to where? Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: We went some 50 or 60 metres away to another building which was right next to the building we were in first, the command or headquarters building, as I call it. And they were the premises of the workers' council of the Kakanj mine. There was a hall there for holding meetings, conferences, and several other rooms, and offices which were used for different purposes in the course of the mine's management, for the management of the mine, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And is it in this room that you were placed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: We were placed in a room next to the workers' council meeting hall, to the left of it. They are adjoining rooms. And they were used for the military archives of the mine. It contained various documents of a military nature, so that the room was well secured. We had provided good security for it previously, for the needs of the Territorial Defence. That meant you had to have iron bars on the windows. We had a steel door. So it was a very secure office, and it was used by the Kakanj mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And as you told us before, you were familiar with this room.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Besides yourself and the other three persons who accompanied you with Jasko, could you tell us if you met anyone else at the room.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that same room or office, as I like to call it, there were already some people there. Some were in uniform; others were civilians. There might have been some 30 or 40 people in that room, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would you be able to assist the Trial Chamber with the ethnic breakdown of the occupants of this room?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them were soldiers of the HVO who were the detainees, or soldiers who had surrendered during a conflict, but mostly they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And, Witness, what was the mood of the occupants of this room when you got there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, there was a conflict going on, and everybody was very depressed. They were all sad, disillusioned, had feelings of consternation. It was not a pleasant sight to see. It was sad to see people feeling like that, pitiful. They looked lost. And of course, that was understandable.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, at this time, how did you feel?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I felt like the rest did, although at the time I started asking myself why I was there with them. But as I say, it's a very unpleasant feeling because all those people knew me and my colleagues, the fellow managers. There were people there to whom we were the managers and directors. They knew us in quite a different light, in quite a different role, so that we found ourselves there together with all the rest of them, and that's not a pleasant feeling.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be correct in saying that you felt confined? Did you feel confined in any way?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, that was the 12th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us and explain to the Trial Chamber what took place the day after the 12th of June, which would have been the 13th of June, 1993, if anything at all took place.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the conflicts were still going on, we could hear the sounds of various weapons being used. Explosions could be heard as well. And all that was very unpleasant. New people were coming in and some others were leaving. There was a lot of coming and going. So that's how the day passed, and that night too. The next day --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you -- excuse me one moment. Were you able to see outside of the room? Could you see outside?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I could not. The distribution of the rooms were such that we weren't able to see what was going on outside on the one side; and on the other side, which is where the windows were, there was a large embankment, so we weren't able to see out there either. We could just tell by the sounds we heard, and they told us what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And who are you referring to when you say "they told us"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Sounds. I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Whom are you referring to when you said "they told us what was going on"? To whom are you referring?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: New people came in and information arrived. Many who were there knew what was going on in their own village and in other villages, and they would convey that to us. So the people coming in would bring in information as to what was going on, so that there were lots of different types of information coming in. Because in situations of that kind, people are always very curious. They listen to hear what was going on. So that's what I meant. And we had some information coming in to us that way. But in the room itself -- from the room itself, we couldn't see anything. All we could do was hear the shots and weapons in the background and perhaps some of what was going on in our immediate vicinity. So that's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, that would have concluded June 13th. Can you recall what would have happened on the 14th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there was a lull by then. The intensity of the military actions was declining. You couldn't hear weapons being fired Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. any more. And there was a lull. There were also fewer soldiers in the compound where we were located. And things quietened down generally. Some of the soldiers who were with us in the room and in the compound were called and taken away. Probably they were released later on. So that we can say that as of the 14th the area began to be depopulated; people began to leave. That's what I experienced.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But you could -- you couldn't see anything from the room, Witness. But could you hear anything coming in from the outside while you were in that room?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Perhaps I ought to add the threats.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: There were several soldiers, soldiers passing by. And when they heard who was being detained on the premises, they wanted to take some -- to effect some sanctions against us. But Jasko wouldn't allow them to do anything to us. He would rush out and prevented them from taking any reprisals. He didn't allow anything like that to happen. But there were threats, of course. They would say things like, "We ought to kill them all," and things like that. But that was the soldiers' frustration because of their own losses, perhaps. It was some sort of frustration on their part for some things that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we come to the 15th of June, 1993. Do you recall how the day began on the 15th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: The day itself began with less intensity, less activity. The camp started to be emptied, and we expected to be released; that is to say, I expected that I would be released. And I was a little astonished that they hadn't let us go the previous day. And we heard on that day already some music in town. And where we were, the premises we were in, about 20 or 30 metres above us was where the road was, so we heard some music coming from a kombi van. And it was louder than it had been previously. I knew the music that was generally played and that sound. It was Islamic music with various things said in Arabic. But you could hear it several times that day, and it was rather strong.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did anything in particular happen around midday of June 15th that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing in particular, except for the fact that the van turned up in front of our prison, or the place that we were incarcerated in. And as I say, you could hear them asking for someone. They were calling out. And then Jasko came into our room and called us, called me. He called to Stjepan too, and I think Komso too, to come and see him in the part that he worked. And we went there and found two soldiers there. I didn't know them, but they asked us to give our names. And Jasko said that -- Jasko told him who we were, and he said that we should follow him and go with them. Jasko said that he hadn't received orders to that effect -- or rather, that his commander had left him in charge of us. So Jasko said he couldn't do anything without the commander's orders. But they started shouting at him and were very strict, but in the end he gave in. They were insistent. I don't know whether anything was signed at this point, but Jasko said that we could now go with them. And that's what we did; we went with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So you left the compound in a bus with the two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a van.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us: Where did this bus take you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: The mini-bus took us round town and went to the parking lot in front of the Sretno Motel. We waited there until some people came out from the motel. This was the Motel Sretno. As I say, some other people arrived in a van, and then all of us together were driven off towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So could we backtrack a moment. On your way to the Motel Sretno, were you able to see what was going on in the streets?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We weren't allowed to look. We had to keep our heads bent with our arms behind our backs, looking at the floor of the kombi, of the van. So we didn't see anything. One of the soldiers was turned towards us, guarding us, while the other was driving. So he didn't permit us to raise our heads to have a quick glance. So I saw nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And tell the Trial Chamber what took place when you got to the Motel Sretno.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: The car stopped in the parking lot. Some soldiers came up to us, opened the door, and told us to wait. We weren't allowed to leave the vehicle or to look around. After some time had passed, several other people came whom we knew, and we were a bit surprised. And we said, "How come you're here, and you too?" And they were loaded up into the van together with us. It was a small van, and we were placed in it like sardines in a tin, one up against another. We weren't allowed to talk amongst others; we weren't allowed to do anything. We had to keep our heads bent, our hands behind our backs. And at one point they closed the doors to the van in the same way, while one of the soldiers was watching us to see that we didn't look around and the other drove us towards Zenica. We knew the road very well. We'd been there thousands of times, so we knew where we were going; we knew what route it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, would you then be able to assist the Trial Chamber as to who took you to the Zenica building? Do you have any idea?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time, no. And I didn't know the people, who they were. They weren't known to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: But at the time, how did they look to you? How were they dressed? How did they look to you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: They were wearing military uniforms. All of them were in camouflage uniforms. I didn't notice any rank insignia or anything like that. You know, in times like that, you don't pay attention, perhaps, to all those details. But I don't think they had any insignia or the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Quite so. Now, you were taken to Zenica. Could you tell us where in Zenica were you taken.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: They took us to what was known as the Music School in Zenica. We arrived in front of the building, got out the same way we had done so before, with our hands behind our backs, our heads bent, looking down at the ground, one by one; went through the entrance to the left, the staircase on the left, and we were all taken into a room there, where we found some other citizens there whom we knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And do you know into whose care you were placed at the Music School?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Not at that time, no. There wasn't any handing over and taking over of us. Quite simply the ones who took us there behaved as if it all belonged to them. They didn't act as if they were handing us over to somebody, to put us in somebody's charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: So you believed there was no one particular person in charge; there wasn't any one particular person.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that moment, I wasn't able to notice anything like that, I was so taken aback.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Can you state for the Trial Chamber the conditions of the room in which you were placed in at the Zenica Music School. Can you describe it and state the conditions for us, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, ten years have passed since then, but I'll tell you to the best of my recollection. It was a room that was about 5 to 6 metres wide, perhaps some 15 metres long. It was a room in the basement, in the cellar. And there were small windows up by the ceiling, looking out onto the street. So it was a cellar, underground, about 2 metres underground. There was just this half metre that was above the surface of the road where there were these little windows. There was some sort of plastic flooring, an oval roof, and I think that -- a vaulted roof. And I think that the Music School used it for some of its -- as a facility for its own purposes, or perhaps they stored something there. Something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Would you be able to assist us further, Witness, with the physical condition of the room? How were you treated -- you know, what was the physical -- were there any amenities? Could you help us?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: In the room, there were some benches or -- well, yes, benches -- which were used by the school, by the pupils. They would put their musical notes or books on them. But you could raise them or lower them. They were benches of about 2 metres long and might have been about 50 centimetres wide, and they had a lid. And there were also some wooden pallets which were used to transport bricks. There were four of those. And there were several chairs too. But they weren't in working order. There was also a bed that you couldn't lie on, things like that, discarded chairs, several blankets. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Toilet facilities? Could you assist us with that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there weren't any toilet facilities at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you used as a toilet?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: We had a plastic pot or container, a 5- or 6-litre container, which we used as a toilet. When it was full, we would ask the guard to let us empty it. They would then allow one of us to go up to the floor and empty it. And that's how we proceeded during our entire stay on the premises.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Approximately how many people would be in the room at any one given time? Approximately how many people?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, there were between 18 and 20 of us. Then some people left; others arrived. And one could say that on average there were between 15 and 18 of us at all times.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And would you be able to assist us with the ethnic breakdown of the occupants of the room at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: They were mostly Croats. There was a Serb who was there all the time. At the beginning there were two Serbs as well, but they left. They were released.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: What would a normal day be like at the Zenica Music School for you at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Since there was no electricity anywhere, neither in the city nor in that building, we had to depend on daylight and on the little light that would reach the basement. We would get up in the morning. We would go to the toilet, et cetera, and we would change. There were always a couple of people who were on duty. They would take out -- they would take the excrement up to the floor. They asked the guards to give us a cloth and water, because sometimes the feces would be spilt in the room, and then we had to clean it up, because we were afraid of infections, of contagious diseases et cetera. We carried out all these activities. Then we would bring water. We had two plastic bottles of a litre and a half or two litres. So there were always two persons who were always responsible for dealing with these matters. The others would remain sitting. They'd be silent. They'd reflect, et cetera. But there were two persons who were responsible for work in all the other premises above us. We would clean up, tidy up, et cetera. And it was our duty, after we had eaten, to clean up, do the washing up, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Now, during the nights, could you describe for us what the nights were like.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: It was completely dark --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to address the Prosecution, to inform them that they have taken over an hour and a half for the examination-in-chief, whereas according to the document, you had planned on examining the witness for an hour. Please try to respect the schedule that has been drawn up. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Much obliged, Mr. President. And I'll soon be finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Whilst at the Zenica Music School, could you indicate to the Tribunal how you were treated.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to answer that question in specific terms. As I have already said, it was very uncomfortable. Living there was very uncomfortable. The occasional interrogations presented another kind of difficulty. Our fate wasn't secure, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, you in particular, could you tell the Tribunal if you were ever interrogated at the Zenica Music School and what transpired.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. After a few days, everyone in fact went to be questioned. So after a few days had passed, I was also called by the manager, by the -- by the warden of the prison. And he took me to be interrogated. I entered the office -- If I may talk about this -- This is how things unfolded.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Yes. Could you briefly tell us exactly how it unfolded, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I entered the office, which was on the second floor, I think. There were two tables placed together, and on one side there was a soldier in uniform and there was another soldier on the other side. They had beards, slightly longish hair. They turned the chair around, so that the back of the chair was facing me. So my back didn't have any support, so to speak. And that's when they started asking me questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. And did anything happen during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When they weren't happy with my answers about some sort of command, and I didn't understand what sort of a command this was, the soldiers who were behind me started kicking me or hitting me with parts of their weapons. I don't know exactly, but I almost lost consciousness. I was out of breath, but they were asking me to answer questions, yet I wasn't capable of answering any questions. I had almost lost consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: For how long would you say this beating lasted?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps for about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. And then were you taken back to your cell?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Okay. Tell the Tribunal the length of period that you stayed at the Zenica Music School. For how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Three months, up until the 29th of September --

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: -- when we were transferred.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you were transferred to.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: We were transferred to what they used to call the correctional facility in Zenica. It used to be a prison in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And you got to Zenica at the prison, the old prison? For how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 23rd of November, which is when I was exchanged. And as a result of this exchange, I was sent to Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: From Zepce, did you go back to Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. There was nowhere for me to go back to. Someone had moved into my flat. Someone had moved into my house. Even if I had wanted to, there was nowhere for me to go, to go back to. And since this wasn't possible, I just waited to see what my fate would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of October, 1994, a convoy from Zepce was organised, which passed through the territory in which the Serbs had a dominant presence. We got as far as Livno. I got off in Livno. We crossed over into Capljina. I greeted my friends there. And then I went to Rijeka to see my brother on the following day, and then I went to see my other brother in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Did you -- do you now live in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I live in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And could you tell us if you will return to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Since I have already organised my life in Zagreb, it is not my intention to return there and live there on a permanent basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. And I have just one more question for you, which eluded me: At the Zenica Music School, you indicated to the Tribunal that people were coming and going and that people were taken for questioning and people were coming and going. Could you tell us if at any time during your stay at the Music School, if you saw people who were taken upstairs coming -- who didn't leave but came back down to the room, and could you tell us, you know, what you saw.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: People would come and go. They'd be beaten. They had bruises. They couldn't walk. They were in a terrible state.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: And in particular, would you be able to tell us the names of these people and what you know about these people, what eventually happened to any one of these, that you may have seen?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: All those who went to be questioned, almost all of them were given a beaten -- beating. Some were beaten more; some a little less. Markic, Andrijevic, and Popovic in particular were badly beaten, as well as Cicak. I could say that my beating wasn't as bad as theirs.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to thank you for your assistance in coming here today.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this is the evidence in chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank the Prosecution. I just have two minor questions for if witness -- the witness before to the Defence to see if they want to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said during the examination-in-chief that you had been beaten. Were you beaten almost every day, or was it occasionally, at intervals?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I was beaten on two occasions: During an interrogation, and on one other occasion, when we were taken away in the van in an unknown direction. We were placed in a room where -- and we were blindfolded so we didn't know where we were. Later we discovered that that was the Bilmiste educational centre. And when we were returning, I was badly beaten. I am speaking about what happened to myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you were transferred to the KP Dom. Were you beaten there?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't beaten, and nor was anyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were questioned, why were you questioned? What was the objective of the questioning? What did they want to find out?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: My interrogators told me that they knew quite a lot about my life; that's one thing. And to be specific, they told me -- or rather, they requested that I admit that I'd been working to have the powerplant and the mine made part of the -- made part of Herceg-Bosna. That was their main accusation. There was a minor accusation that had to do with explosives. Since we are a mining company, I told them that I wasn't responsible for explosives in the mine. I told them that other people were responsible for explosives there, because I was involved in investment and development and not in concrete, logistical tasks. And since they beat me, I wasn't in a position to provide them with sensible answers. The prison warden later said that I had to write down my answers. They provided me with a pen and paper and even a candle, and I answered that question and the others. There were three questions: There was one that concerned Herceg-Bosna; another that concerned explosives; and there was another, a third question, that wasn't that important. I wrote my answers down and handed it over to the prison warden. Later I wasn't summoned again or questioned with regard to that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My very last question: When you were in the Music School, were you guarded by civilians or members of the military?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the soldiers who were present, did you identify them? Did you know the units that they belonged to, or were you not able to identify them?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a military police station, and soldiers would come and go all the time. So it was very rare for a soldier to remain there for more than several days. The soldiers kept changing, kept rotating, so I assumed that this was the military police of the 7th Muslim Brigade, because they had regular ritual rites -- religious rites which were performed there. They had a summons to pray every day and they would go up to the top because I know there was an area where they would pray there. I know that because I went to clean the place when they were performing these religious rites. It was silent. There was silence there. And that's how I knew that it belonged to that unit, because I knew that in the army units no such religious rites were performed; at least, not as far as I am aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have another ten minutes before the break. Does the Defence want to start with the cross-examination and continue after the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think it would be appropriate to start with our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Tvrtkovic. My name is Edina Residovic, and I'm representing General Enver Hadzihasanovic. I have a number of questions for you that relate to your testimony before this Trial Chamber. I'd like to ask you whether it is true that in 2002 you gave a statement to investigators from The Hague Tribunal about these events.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to your personal position in Kakanj, you have provided the Trial Chamber some general indications about the overall situation. I think it is important to understand what you have been testifying about. So would this -- in this regard, I would like to ask you a number of questions. Have I understood you correctly: You were born in Kakanj and up until June 1993 you lived in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before -- just before the war, you didn't join a single national party that came to power; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given your professional and social engagements, you had a fairly high social position in the mine and in the municipality as a whole; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But although the war broke out, you weren't mobilised into any military structure present in the municipality at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, in accordance with the law, you were employed and you were a member of the war staff of the mine by virtue of your position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The duties you had to perform in the mine didn't leave you much time to follow all the events in your community and beyond; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But given that the media relayed the events that were taking place in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you heard that in the wider area of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1993 an armed conflict between the BH Army and the HVO had broken out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, it seemed to you, on account of the peaceful situation in Kakanj, that such a conflict would not break out in your community; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said in the course of your testimony - and I would like you to confirm this - that it was clear to you that the mine, its productivity, and the work of the plant, of the powerplant in Kakanj, was of extreme importance for the entire state and for the military structures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that in the spring of 1993 a member of the BH Presidency, Ejup Ganic, came to Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All the representatives of political structures in the municipality and of commercial organisations and of the military structures of the BH Army and the HVO were called to the meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You attended that meeting and you know that all those who attended it, apart from the representatives of the HVO, were there, which was a bit strange for you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew that the HVO, according to the law, was part of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it didn't recognise the Presidency command but it obeyed orders that were issued to it from its headquarters in Grude; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I can say is that there were certain disagreements. But as to the nature and the form of these disagreements, I couldn't say what they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although you did not follow the situation carefully, the situation in the general area, you nevertheless knew that at the beginning of June in the surrounding villages of the municipality of Kakanj a conflict or clashes broke out between the army and the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure about a lot of conflicts, but I know about a conflict in the village of Lucici, which is -- which is when a large-scale conflict broke out in the municipality of Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me whether the village of Poljani is in the municipality of Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that at the beginning of June there was a massacre against the inhabitants, the Bosniak inhabitants of that village, and those bodies were partially burnt? The police and the Ministry of the Interior from Kakanj carried out the on-site investigation. Did you hear anything about this incident? If not --

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not claiming that it did not happen, but I cannot remember it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Only tell us what you know about. At the beginning of 1993, given your duties, you went on official trips through Western Herzegovina as well and with a colleague who was a HVO member. You went on these trips and you had the opportunity of meeting Mate Boban on one such occasion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, Mate Boban was the President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will interrupt the Defence for a moment. Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution opposes this line of questioning. It goes far beyond the scope of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. With regard to the scope of the cross-examination, you know that we have been provided with a motion in order to specify what the scope was. We said that it was necessary to adhere to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Rule 90. You must concentrate on the subjects addressed by the Prosecution and you must concentrate on the credibility of the witness. So it's necessary to place the responses within the context. We have noticed that the witness said that he wasn't aware of the context, so the impression we have is that the questions you are asking are not useful because the witness said that he didn't know the answer. So we are going to break because of technical reasons. That will allow us to think about what has just been said during the break. We will resume with the cross-examination of the witness at ten past 4.00. And I'd like to ask the Prosecution to respect the timing for the second witness, to the extent that this is possible. It would be good to finish with both witnesses by 7.00. We will adjourn now and after the break, at 4.10, the Defence can continue with its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, I'd like to say that the question to which the Prosecution first objected might have been my question when I asked him whether he knew about a conflict in a village. Now, as we have the witness statement in our possession, and we know the things that he talked about there, we based our questions on that statement in order to confirm that that was so. So that was the groundwork for our question. He confirmed the first fact but said didn't know about the other one. Now, if there was an objection to my second question, the second question related to his meeting or, rather, his presence at a meeting where he got to know Mate Boban. That is something that the witness confirmed, and it is also a question he mentioned earlier on. So this is to test the credibility of the witness as to that fact. Mr. President, I have two or three more questions left to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Withopf, before I give you the floor, the Defence would like to say that they are cross-examining the witness on the basis of what he said in his written statement. So the first question was a question relating to that statement. You objected. The Prosecution objected. So we wanted to compare this with the written document. And the second question had to do with a meeting at which the witness participated, in view of his local functions and positions, et cetera. And I think that the question could be asked of the witness quite rightly, because he was a prominent individual in Kakanj. As an intellectual, as a mining engineer, and otherwise. So he could have taken part in administrative meetings. And therefore, it would be normal for us to be able to ask him those questions. I should also like to add that when I asked him, I asked him why he was being interrogated, what they wanted to find out. And he told me what the purpose of the interrogations were. So that was a link. Now, would you nonetheless like to take the floor at this point, Mr. Withopf?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President, Your Honours. I think there are two issues involved. The first one is the issue as to whether the prior statement actually determines the scope of the cross-examination. Rule 90(H)(i) only refers to the evidence in chief and not to the previous witness statement. And the second issue is the relevance of the questions as put by the Defence to the witness. At this point in time, I can't see the relevance of such questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not say that the previous statement was a framework for the cross-examination. The prior statement is something that the Defence can use to test the credibility of the witness. And in case the witness deviates considerably from what he said, then we can refer to the prior statement. I think that the witness gave me very precise and specific answers to the questions I asked him, and I thank him for that. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We won't go back to that question, because you said you happened to be present at the meeting by chance -- not meeting -- or rather, the place where you met Mr. Mate Boban. That's all I asked you. And you asserted that.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I confirmed that. But may I just add something and clarify this point? The people I travelled with were having a meeting. They had the meeting. And all they did was to ask me whether I wanted to meet Mr. Boban. And I said that yes, I did, because I'm always a curious man and I was interested in meeting him, because at the time he was somebody who was a prominent political figure. So I had this opportunity, and we just talked to him. And if you would like me to say what we talked about, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tvrtkovic. I just asked you that question in order to bring up my next question: Is it true and correct that during the time you were interrogated at the Music School you were asked about that meeting, they asked you about it? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tvrtkovic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just turn to the Defence. So you asked him about -- a question about Mr. Boban. The Chamber does not know who Mr. Boban is. So perhaps you could have incorporated into your question, "Did you meet Mr. Boban, who was so and so?" because just by simply says "Mr. Boban" doesn't tell me anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tvrtkovic, shall we assist the Trial Chamber. At the time, Mr. Mate Boban, who is deceased now, was at the time president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and president of the HVO. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And at that time, the army was in conflict with the HVO; is that right? During the time you were at the Music School, I mean.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in Kakanj. It is difficult for me to say whether it was in conflict elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mostar, Central Bosnia. Never mind. But you know the conflicts ended in February 1994 with the Washington Agreement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we only have three or four questions and won't take up much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tvrtkovic, during today's testimony, you said that you left the Music School on the 29th of September, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: The 20th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the investigators, you said that you left the Music School on the 20th of August. And I have a confirmation here from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So could it have been the 20th of August? You allow for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Many years have gone by since then. I know it was the 20th, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the individual who interrogated you or questioned you at the Music School, his name was Jasmin Ismic, is it? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: I heard the name many, many years later; however, at that time, I did not know what that person's name was, nor did I know anything about the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The third question would be as follows: While you were in Kakanj in the mine, the mine premises, you were able to receive visits.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm not receiving the interpretation, but I can hear you without the headsets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question. During the time you spent in Kakanj at the mine's premises, before you went to the Music School, your nearest and dearest, your friends were able to visit you, and your relatives too.

utterances.speaker: IVAN MILJENKO TVRTKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any redirect by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, no re-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, at the request of the Prosecution, you came here and answered questions put to you by the Prosecution and by the Defence. The Chamber would like to thank you for giving testimony and we wish you bon voyage back to your own country. I'll now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before introducing the second witness, I would like to ask the registrar - and this is only going to take a few moments - if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And with the break and the cross-examination, I think we can be finished by 7.00 p.m. Of course, if the questions are pertinent ones, well-focussed on the facts. The usher is looking for the witness. Yes, the witness is coming into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the witness is taking his seat, first let me say good afternoon to Your Honour, and to my colleagues. In light of what the President has just said, the Prosecution anticipates that this witness will take approximately one hour on direct examination, rather than the 1.5 hours indicated, so I don't anticipate any problems meeting the schedule as set forth by Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, can you hear the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please give us your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ranko Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 25th of December, 1944.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where? Which locality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Donji Vijacani, the Prnjavor municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your present job? Are you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not employed, but I am a telecommunications engineer by profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. And where is your place of residence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I live in Prnjavor, and that is my native town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are now going to read the text of the solemn declaration. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter] Pz

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated. Sir, you're now going to be answering questions asked by the Prosecution, and they are sitting to your right. Afterwards, you will be answering questions put to you by the Defence, and they are to your left. You have the Judges in front of you, and they, too, will be asking you questions. You have been called here to testify about the facts that you personally saw, those that you were an eyewitness to, or events that took place and things you heard about and experienced. It would be helpful if you would give longer answers and not just yes or no answers, so complete answers. Let me tell you that the Judges sitting in front of you know nothing about what you're going to be asked about, so the examination-in-chief will help us arrive at the truth, and therefore you're going to be asked specific questions about the things you saw. If there is something that is not quite clear to you, please ask to hear the question again. Having said that, I'm now going to give the floor to the representatives of the Prosecution, without further ado, for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you please tell us where you were living in 1992.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I was living and working in Kakanj at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did you move to Kakanj? What year?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I moved to Kakanj from Zenica in 1969. It was August, I believe. I worked there at the steelworks of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us in 1992 what the approximate population of Kakanj was.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, the overall population of the city of Kakanj in 1992, roughly, if you know.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'd rather start with the ethnic composition. Eight to nine per cent were Serbs; about 18 per cent were Croats; and the rest I can't -- the Bosniaks, or Muslims, might have made up 56 per cent. I can't be quite sure. But most of them were workers, part of the working class, working in the large enterprises in Kakanj or the smaller ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many people lived in the city of Kakanj in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those are facts and figures and statistics. I have heard of them, but Kakanj had between 12 and 15 thousand inhabitants. And the Kakanj municipality numbered about 50 or 53 thousand inhabitants. But don't hold it to me exactly. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, what is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb. I'm a Serb. That's my ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Witness, when a state of war or armed conflict broke out in the area around Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: That happened in 1993, I believe. Yes, 1993. Sometime in June. So that means in June. But not in the town itself; I know that for a fact. It was the area outside the town, around the town. Not in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In June of 1993, Witness, were you employed? And if so, where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was employed in the thermoelectric powerplant of Kakanj. And as there wasn't much work at the time, we were placed at the company's disposal. You were actually at home; you would receive a reduced salary. And when the need arose and when there was work to do, they would call you and you would go to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Witness, when the war or armed conflict actually broke out in the town of Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not in town, no. There wasn't a conflict in the town. At least -- well, I was there, so I would know. No, it didn't happen. Not in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Witness, when there were any offences directed at the town of Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: That was then, that day, when the armed conflict started. But as I say, it wasn't on a large scale. It wasn't a large offensive with any artillery, mortars, and so on. I can't be quite specific, of course, because you weren't able to go outside. For security reasons, there was a general alarm that was sounded. But perhaps one or two grenades exploded. Where they came from, I don't know. You could hear them, but you couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've made reference to "that day, when the armed conflict started." Do you have a recollection of the specific day upon which the armed conflict started?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I think I do, but I'm not quite sure. I think it was on the 9th of June. But don't hold me to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in which year was that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what you were doing and where you were on the day the armed conflict started in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As the alarm was sounded, you weren't allowed to leave your house. And I was at home when the alarm went off. That would be it. So not -- the whole day and the whole evening you weren't allowed to leave your home -- we weren't allowed to leave our homes for our safety and security. Because there was always the danger of a stray bullet or stray shell hitting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of residence did you live in in June 1993 when the armed conflict started?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I was in a flat, a three-room flat in the centre of Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On what floor was your flat located in this building?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: On the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you able to see what was occurring in the town of Kakanj from your first-floor flat?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, you couldn't see that, because the configuration of the terrain in the town itself and in the surrounding parts is that Kakanj lies in a valley, so you can only see 1 or 2 hundred metres in front of you or to the left or right. It's in a river valley. All you can do is hear what's going on. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What could you hear from your first-floor flat as the conflict began in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: You could hear infantry fire. And whether they were mortars or the artillery or whatever, but you could hear that sort of thing, although I'm not an expert. All I know is that some of that was going on but I don't think nothing hit the town of Kakanj itself. Perhaps just one or two shells. But I didn't see that happen. As I say, you weren't allowed to leave your house. You could only hear what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once the armed conflict in Kakanj began, how much longer did you remain in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
