utterances.text: You mean how many days?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once the -- yes. How many days after the armed conflict began did you remain living in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I lived there until the 18th of June of that same year, which means 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Between the beginning of the armed conflict on or about the 9th of June, 1993, until the 18th of June, 1993, did you on any occasion leave your apartment for any reason?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Because you had to go and buy food and the basic essentials. No other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On those occasions, in that time period when you left your apartment, did you see any soldiers on the streets of Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were these soldiers wearing?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see, for the amount of time they were on the road they were wearing the normal camouflage uniform, and all of them had infantry weapons. You could see that. Of course, you weren't able to see very much. Whenever there was a crowd, you didn't dilly-dally. You did what you had to do and went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know which army or armed forces the soldiers that you saw on the streets in Kakanj belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what can I say? I know they were soldiers belonging to the BH Army. I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw them. I saw them on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see any indications on their uniforms that led you to believe that they were members of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say, because ... Well, I didn't spend much time in the streets, so I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned the 18th of June, 1993, Witness. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, at around 14.10 hours, somebody rang my doorbell, and I thought that it was a friend whom I was expecting, so I opened the door. But to my astonishment, I saw two armed soldiers standing there, and they came inside and asked me if they -- they said they wanted to take a look around the apartment. At first I was a little taken aback, confused. I didn't know what was going on. But they asked me to show them my radio station. I said I didn't have one, that I had handed it over in 1992 to the SUP of Kakanj and that I have a receipt to prove it. And that's what happened. There was a general announcement from the local radio station in Kakanj that all radio hams - and I was a radio ham myself - should turn over, hand in their radio stations. And I did so; so did a colleague of mine, Franjo, who lived in the same building. He also had a radio station. And another man called Mile. I've forgotten his surname. So they all took their radio stations and took them to the SUP. We all did that. We packed them up nicely, because they told us to pack them up. And they gave us receipts. So they asked to see the receipt. And I said the receipt's in my car. So we went downstairs to my car, and I gave them the receipt. But they weren't actually interested in the receipt - I don't know why - what they wanted was the my car keys and the keys to the garage. And they ordered me to enter the van. There were two soldiers. They ordered me into the van, and then they drove me off with them to the motel. It's a motel at the crossroads on the Zenica-Sarajevo main road. So that's where the motel was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you a couple of follow-on questions. You've told us about two soldiers. What were these soldiers wearing?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms. They had infantry weapons. I don't know what the type of weapons they -- what type of weapons they were. They were from the units of the 7th Muslim Brigade, as it was called, and it was their police, actually. And what was I going to say? Ah, yes, in Kakanj everyone referred to them as MOS, as the MOS men. So the abbreviation was used. They were soldiers from the MOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, how do you know that these soldiers were from the 7th Muslim Brigade or the MOS?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say that was a public secret. Everyone knew about the MOS taking prisoners away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once you -- you told us that you were ordered into a van. Can you describe what the van looked like or what type of van it was.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: It was a green van. I think it had an irregular pattern on it, a sort of camouflage pattern. It was a standard van. I think it was a TAM van with about eight seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, at the time these two soldiers took you or put you into this van, were you serving as a member of any armed force?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you weren't serving as a member of the HVO or the VRS or any other type of military organisation.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us that they took you to a motel at the crossroads on the Zenica-Sarajevo main road. Do you know the name of that motel?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: The name of the motel was Motel Sretno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask at this point that the witness be shown the electronic copy of Prosecution Exhibit 10.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the motel. I think this is a recent photograph, because in the right-hand corner a large circular sign is missing with the inscription "Motel Sretno." It's probably renovated. And it didn't say "hotel"; it said "motel." There was a large circular sign on the right side of the facade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, other than the changes that you've just told us about, does the building that's depicted in Prosecution Exhibit 10, that should be on the screen in front of you, does that resemble the building, Motel Sretno, as it was in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how far from your apartment in Kakanj was the Motel Sretno?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: A kilometre and a half to 2 kilometres at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, prior to your arrival at the Motel Sretno on June 18th, 1993, did you have any knowledge as to what that motel was being used for?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were rumours in Kakanj, according to which the motel was being used as a kind of prison. That's what people were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time of day you arrived at the hotel on 18 June 1993?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was arrested on the 14th of October, so it could have been at half past 2.00 or 3.00 on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the -- at least, the English translation indicated that you were arrested on the 14th of October. Can you tell us again the date that you were arrested and taken from your flat to the Motel Sretno.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where that date has appeared from, but it was on the 18th of June, 1993. I will remember that for as long as I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And to the best of your recollection, you arrived there sometime between half past 2.00 and 3.00 on 18 June 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened upon your arrival at the Motel Sretno, starting with when the van, the kombi, arrived at the motel.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to go over that again now, but I'll have to. They took me out of the van. They took me to some basement rooms in the motel. When the motel was being used, there were some sort of cubicles there, 2 by 2 metres, and there was a group of soldiers there. As soon as I got there, they started beating me immediately with everything they could. I tried to avoid the blows and protect my back by approaching the wall, getting closer up to the wall, and I'd use my hands to shield my face, to the extent that this is possible. It's difficult to say how long this lasted. In such situations, time doesn't mean anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall approximately how many soldiers were present at the time you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were six of them, six soldiers. There was a line of six soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were the soldiers wearing?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if you saw any distinctive badges, patches, or other components of the uniforms that might have led you to know what unit or military they were associated with?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On their sleeves here they had a sort of attachment, something attached to the sleeve, and they had an inscription that was printed on their sleeves, on both arms, on the left arm and on the right arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what the inscription that was printed on their sleeves said or indicated?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say what it said exactly, because there wasn't any light in the basement and it wasn't possible to see things clearly. So I can't say for certain that I saw certain things. Later, they said these inscriptions were the inscriptions of the 7th Brigade. These were the inscriptions they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you said upon arrival they started beating you. Do you recall what they were using, what instruments they were using to beat you with upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They kicked us. They'd punch us. There were cables that they would use, short cables, about half a metre long. I don't know whether they were plastic or of some other material. That's -- that's what they used to beat us with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned cubicles in the basement of the Motel Sretno. Can you describe these cubicles for the Trial Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can, because I spent quite a lot of time there, so I can provide you with the details. It was some sort of a temporary warehouse. There were two or three of them, one after the other. And let's say the dimensions were 2 metres by 2 metres. They had some sort of protection in front of them, some sort of wooden bars. There was a -- at the top of the hall, there were some metal bars, and to the left there was another cubicle of that kind and to the right there was such a cubicle. They were used as storage space, and they were more or less the same size, all of these cubicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Upon your arrival at Motel Sretno in the basement on the 18th of June, 1993, were there any other civilians being detained in the basement of that building at the time you arrived?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't see any civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the basement of the Motel Sretno, after your arrival on the 18th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I remained there on the following day and the day after that, so two complete days, until the afternoon, until the third day, until about midday, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the three days that you remained in the basement of the Motel Sretno, were any other civilians brought to the basement and detained there?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A young man, who was about 30 or 35 years old, was brought in. He was a civilian. And he was imprisoned together with me in what we could call a cell. That was on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than this young man and yourself, during the three days that you were there, was anyone else, any other civilians detained in the basement of the Motel Sretno?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. There were just the two of us, while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the three days that you were detained in the basement of the Motel Sretno, were you taken out of the cubicle that you were being detained in for any purpose?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was taken out so that I could wash myself and so I could eat because there was a canteen, a sort of temporary canteen that was a little before that cubicle. And so yes, I was taken out to eat and to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any time were you taken out for any type of interrogation or questioning while you were kept at the Motel Sretno?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point in time after your arrival, were you -- you've told us about being beaten upon arrival. Were there any incidents after that where you were physically mistreated?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that happened on the following day. In the afternoon, none of the soldiers were present. I think that only one of the soldiers was in the hall. They called me to come to the bars of the prison and to lean against the bars. He then took some sort of wooden implement which is used to cover houses with, and then he would hit me on the head. He would do this through the bars. He did it several times. Luckily the wooden implement broke. That was just one of the soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's probably an interpretation error, since the witness said again that it was just one soldier. At line 17 -- no, 16 -- it says "they called me." And that would mean that there were several of them. Whereas the witness said "he called me." So if this could be corrected immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So could the Prosecution ask the witness again whether there was just one soldier who was present there or whether there were several of them, because in line 17 it appears to be ambiguous, since the Defence heard something else in the B/C/S version. So could we ask the witness again to correct this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, on this occasion that you're telling us about, where you were leaning against the bars, was there one soldier present or more than one soldier present?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I was facing that soldier, and only one soldier was present. I think he was on duty or something like that. There was just one soldier who did that. I don't know how this translation error occurred, but there was only one soldier who was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than the time when you were mistreated upon your arrival at the Motel Sretno and this incident which you've just described involving one soldier, were there any other occasions during the time you were detained at the Motel Sretno where you were physically mistreated?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, there was no other -- there were no other occasions on which I was mistreated in Motel Sretno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber any physical injuries that you received as a result of these beatings in the basement of the Motel Sretno.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Because of the last time -- because of the last time I was beaten by this soldier, I was covered in blood. I don't have a medical report about this, but there are visible traces on my head. There are scars. But as for the rest, well, there were bruises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The blood that you've told us about, do you know where on your body that blood came from?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: From my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time you were detained in the basement of the Motel Sretno, Witness, did you observe the young man who was detained with you being mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But I have to emphasise that that soldier wanted us to fight each other. We had to do that. But I must say that we -- we acted this out. You know how it looks. He'd hit me, and then I'd hit him. These weren't blows of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've told us, Witness, that you remained in the Motel Sretno for three days. Where did you go at the end of that three-day period?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: After that - and I remember this well - I was covered in blood. They put me in the van together with another civilian. And I was a civilian too. They put us in the van. We didn't know where we were going. When we took the road, I realised we were going to Kakanj, to the town. We didn't know what was going to happen. And when we arrived at the entrance over the bridge, to the first building, they stopped and they said that -- they told this person to get out. I saw that they were releasing him. And they then turned around and continued with me as far as Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know who this other civilian that was with you in the kombi was, the one that they released? Do you know who he was or where he came from?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know him. He was a young man, 30, 35 years old. He said that he was a bulldozer operator and that he worked on some sort of sparse road. I didn't have the opportunity to ask him what it was. But he was building a road somewhere. And I assume that that is why they released him without any complications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was this the same man that you had been detained in the basement with, this civilian that they released?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the same young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us just a moment ago that they continued with you as far as Zenica. How far is it from Kakanj to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: The exact distance between Kakanj and Zenica is 28 kilometres, up to the junction. And if you add the distance that you have to drive through the town, it's another kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time you arrived in Zenica on that day?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It may have been after 12.00, at about half past 12.00 because the soldiers who were in the Music School, they had just finished lunch. So most of the soldiers were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you just mentioned the Music School. In fact, is that where they took you in the kombi on the 21st of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the building. I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the witness now be shown the electronic copy of Prosecution Exhibit 7, if that could be put on the monitor for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The building that you see, Prosecution Exhibit 7, is the Zenica Music School. Is that what you're saying, Witness?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened once you arrived at the Zenica Music School on the 21st of June, 1993, at about 12.00 or 12.30 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I have already said, it was lunchtime and a lot of soldiers were leaving the canteen. The van stopped in front of the building, right in front of the building. And I remember this well. They took me into the building then. At the entrance to the building, there were bars. Naturally, the entrance was open. And when they had taken me inside, one of the soldiers - I don't know who - immediately cried out, "Here is a Chetnik." And then the beating started. It was a line of soldiers up to the entrance into the basement of the Music School and everyone would deal me a blow with whatever he could get his hands on. I was most frequently kicked. This continued until I entered the basement, because the basement was immediately to the left, perhaps at a distance of 2 or 3 metres, and then there was a sort of a landing, and then you would descend into the basement. So this gauntlet of soldiers is the one that I had to run through, and then they beat me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall approximately how many soldiers constituted this gauntlet?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's difficult to say how many of them there were exactly, but not less than ten soldiers. It's difficult to provide the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were these soldiers wearing?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms, and some of them were also wearing black uniforms, uniforms that were completely black.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you saw any patches, insignia, or other identifying features of these uniforms that might have led you to conclude what unit or military organisation they were associated with?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I have already said, they had these attachments on their sleeves, on both sleeves. And let's say there were some sort of inscriptions on them. But when there's such a confusion and you're being beaten by everyone it's impossible to remember this or to notice what the inscription is. They don't allow you to look. They always tell you to bend your head. I don't know why. Probably to prevent someone from identifying something or seeing something, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Witness, can you tell the Trial Chamber, if you recall, what type of instrument or instruments you were beaten with upon arrival at the Music School.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I have already said, it was mostly their shoes. So they would kick us. Then they'd use their rifle butts. And there were these rubber or plastic cables. I can't be sure whether it was rubber or plastic, but they used pieces of cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did this beating occur for upon your arrival?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: It happened immediately. As soon as I entered the hall of the Music School, it started immediately. As to how long it lasted, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once you went through this gauntlet, witness, where did you then or where were you then taken?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you turned left, that led to the basement, so -- to the basement of the Music School. There was a classroom that was part of the Music School there. I came across quite a lot of civilians down there. I didn't know who they were immediately, because it was dark, because the windows were very small and it was in the basement and there wasn't much light. I couldn't get used to the dark. All I know is that they said, "Pop, how is it that you have ended up here?" Because that's what they would call me, Pop, on the basis of my last name. It took me a while, half an hour, to figure out who was down in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, how many civilians were detained in the basement of the Zenica Music School when you arrived there on the 21st of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: After that, when I came to and felt better, I saw that they were all -- well, not all of them, but that they were from Kakanj. There were a lot of people I knew, colleagues of mine from Kakanj, and there were a total of 11 of them, 11 whom I found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So once you joined them, there was a total of 12; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Of these 11 men that were there, how many of them did you know from before?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you them all. There was Cicak Ilija, Ilija Cicak; Ivica Andrijevic; Tvrtkovic Ivica; Franci Zupancic, I knew him; then there was another engineer whom I didn't know, his name was Stjepan. Those are the ones I knew. Oh, yes, there was another one called Dane Majic, I knew him because he worked with me at the powerplant. And there was someone else, but he was released very quickly. His named was Cvijanovic. I can't remember his first name. I know that his father's name is Ranko. So those are the ones I knew personally. And that's why they said, "How come you're here, Pop?" And I said, "Well, here I am." I didn't know the others, but we got to know each other, talking to each other, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, how long were you kept in the basement of the Zenica Music School following your arrival on 21 June 1993?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in the Music School? Is that the question? How long --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, how long were you detained in the Music School?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 20th of August -- yes, the 20th of August. Of that same year, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber any instances after your arrival where you were physically mistreated while detained at the Music School.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the first beating - and we called that, well, allegedly, our welcoming - that was two or three days later. In the evening hours, a guard turned up. At least they called him the guard, but he was the prison warden, and call me out to go upstairs on the first floor. And I knew what was coming, what was in store for me. I don't think there was any electricity that night. There were just some candles that had been lit. And they took me up to the first floor of the Music School and into an office there. There was a writing table in the office and a man sitting at the table. And there were four soldiers there too. They ordered me to sit down on the chair, and then the interrogation started. They asked me to tell them where my radio station was, who I was connected to, and what my code was. I said I didn't have a radio station, that I had handed it back and that I can't give you a code or anything else, because I haven't got one. But that wasn't enough for him, and they began beating me. There were four of them. One of them was wearing a black uniform. I remember that. That remains in my mind because it instilled the greatest fear. And that's when the beating started. And they started beating me with whatever they had at hand. One of them beat me with one of these rifles that they called the Pumperica with the barrel and I had a injury from that, a scar. And the rest cruised what they had, the rubber cable, they kicked me, they beat me with their fists. And how long did that last? Well, I can't say exactly. Because it's difficult to say how long things like that last when you're actually there. You're very frightened. You have to fight for your survival, so you can't give an exact time. But I was really very well beaten up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of physical injuries did you sustain as a result of this beating?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: After I was beaten, they took me off, and the only thing I was worried about was that I would fall unconscious, because then I couldn't know what they were going to do to me. They threw me into the basement, and all my colleagues rushed up to see what had happened to me. I found it difficult to walk and stand, but I did manage to stand up. I'm not a very strong man otherwise, but I did manage to stand on my own two feet. They gave me some water. I think Ivica was the name of a man who gave me a cigarette. Although, I'm not a smoker, he gave me a cigarette. So I lit it and smoked. Now, as to the injuries, they were bruises. I was all black and blue all over my back, all black and blue. And they put damp cloths over my injuries, bandaged me up and so on. But there wasn't -- there wasn't any blood, just the bruises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On any other occasion before you were taken away from the Music School were you physically mistreated, other than your -- upon your arrival and this incident that you've just been describing for us?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you witness any of the other men detained in the basement of the Music School being physically mistreated?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: All I could see was when they -- what they looked like when they came back, having been beaten. So I was an eyewitness to what they looked like afterwards. I saw their injuries, just as they had seen the injuries on my own body. And I think that's quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To your recollection, were any of the other men who were detained with you during this period in the basement of the Zenica Music School spared such physical mistreatment?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: I've forgotten a little, how it was, but I'm remembering -- trying to remember. At one point, after my own arrival, two other young men were brought in. One of them might have been about 25. And he was wounded in his eye. Actually, he didn't have one eye, and he was brought in from the hospital. And he said that he had lost his eye in some fighting, in an armed struggle. The second young guy didn't have a leg. He was brought in from the battlefield and from the hospital too, where he lost his leg. So according to them - although, I didn't feel this - but I didn't see any physical mistreatment of those two. That's a fact. They just took them up to be questioned and things like that. But I didn't see any traces of physical abuse, nor did they say they had been beaten or mistreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than these two individuals that you've just described, of the original 11 people that were there when you got there were they all physically mistreated during the time you were at the Music School?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know during the time you were in the basement of the Zenica Music School whether any international observers entered that building?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the journalist who was with us from Kakanj, this man called Franci Zupancic understood English. And at one point he said, "Just a second. Somebody is speaking English." And then he said that there were people from the International Red Cross. And that happened twice. So they did come there in intervals of 20 days, but they didn't actually come down into the basement, to the room where we were in. Now, why not I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you describe for the Trial Chamber the living conditions that you endured in the basement of the Zenica Music School during the period you were detained there.

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. It was a room, let us say 8 times 15 in size. And there were some plastic tiles on the floor. And we had to clean them, the detainees. So it was clean because it was in our best interest to keep it clean, for health reasons. At the other end of the classroom were the school benches, the kind you would find in any school. And there were some army blankets and some sponge mattresses that we silent on, foam mattresses or whatever. So we kept the place as clean as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about access to food or drinking water? What was that like?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: As far as drinking water, we did have drinking water; not a lot of it, but we had enough for our requirements. We would go up onto the floor above to wash ourselves. As to food, we did have food. Of course, we didn't have any choice, nor was it a lot, but as we kept the canteen clean too, we could see that they didn't have much more either. So we were more or less equals there; they didn't have a lot and we didn't have a lot either. But they gave us enough to keep us alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have access to either showers or bathtubs during the two-month period you were there?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, there were no bathtubs or showers. There was just a row of taps and sort of wash basins. And we could wash there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, did you have in the basement, in the room that you were kept in, was there a toilet that you could use?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, there wasn't a toilet. If we needed to go to the toilet, the guard would let us go outside and up onto the floor above. They were always ready to do that when there weren't any soldiers there, because they knew what we could expect if there were any soldiers around. So they were okay guys in that respect. But we also had a bucket for urinating in, not to have to leave the room, for our own safety for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, finally, you've mentioned on a few occasions that you had had before you were arrested and detained a radio and that you had turned that in. Do you recall the month and year that you turned in your radio?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: I turned the radio in straight away, at the beginning of the war. That might have been May 1992. So at the beginning of the war, that's when I turned it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say in this context, "the beginning of the war," you mean the greater war in Bosnia, not the war that began in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, the greater war, the beginning of the actual war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions at this time for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, I have two or three questions to ask you myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We listened with great care and attention to the answers you gave to the questions asked, and you said that when you were captured in your apartment that the reason was that the two soldiers, who came to your apartment, wanted to check whether you had returned your radio station. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When you were detained in the Sretno Motel, you were hit by a soldier, and the blows that you received for you, were they individual blows or was that the general modus operandi? Was that what the soldiers did generally? Did the soldiers get out of control and start beating the person that they had control of, or do you think that it was systematic?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer that, but this soldier was alone, so I assume that it was something individual that he did and not systematic. He himself decided to beat me. I don't know what else was happening around me, but that's what happened to me. And I don't know whether that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Now, with respect to your two-month detention, you were subjected to interrogation, and that apparently was once again linked to the question of the radio station and the code. Did they think you were a spy? Was that the sense of their interrogation? Did they think you were a spy, in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was it, nothing more than that. Because it just all boiled down to one question: Do you have a radio or don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were -- how many times were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: At the Music School, I was just interrogated once; that night, as I described earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You said that you were subjected to beatings and blows. In your opinion, the people who did the beating, did they seem to be following orders or once again did that seem to be on their own bat, at their own initiative, or were those individuals acting pursuant to some orders?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Now it is twenty-five minutes to 6.00. I think that the best thing would be to take our regular break, which we have to do anyway, for the technicians to be able to change the tape - if there are no further questions, of course -- perhaps the Defence doesn't have any further questions. No cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. Popovic. I should like to say that General Hadzihasanovic's Defence has no questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we just have a few questions. It will take no more than five minutes, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we have the technical possibility to do so, may we continue for those five minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that ought to be technically possible, as we know your ability to synthesise. Go ahead with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tvrtkovic --

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not Tvrtkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Popovic. I am Mr. Kubura's Defence counsel. And I have a few questions to ask you with respect to this afternoon's testimony. While you were at the Music School, during those two months, were members of your family able to visit you?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me tell you. Yes, they did have the right to visit us, and people were able to bring in food. I myself did not have any close relatives there. I just had an aunt living in Zenica. And she wasn't well off. But yes, he would bring me in things from time to time. However, the rest of the detainees from Kakanj had large families and relatives, and they were allowed to bring in food to the detainees. Let me also state that when they brought in the food, there was just a routine checkup to see that it was only food that was being brought in. And the food was given to us. And let me also add that we -- they also -- we were also allowed to send out our dirty underwear and clothing to cleaned and a fresh change of clothes to be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: One more question: When you described the person who interrogated you at the Music School, you said in your prior statement to the investigators of the Tribunal that it was an individual who was thin, with a small beard, and you said that his name was Jasmin Ismic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know him at the time. None of the detainees knew that person at the time. But I don't know. Somehow they learnt what his name was. Whether just by chance, because they would call -- the soldiers would call out -- not soldiers, the people would call out to each other. So that's how they came to know his name. Otherwise, none of us detainees knew who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, could you just tell me whether that was the man in question, according to what you learnt later on?

utterances.speaker: RANKO POPOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't actually say, but the people said that that was his name. The others said that that was his name. But nobody saw him after that. I left; everybody else left; we all went our separate ways, so I didn't give it much thought afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Judges would like to thank you for coming into court to testify. I'm going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom, and we wish you bon voyage and return to your country.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I am glad if I have managed to help you in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has no further questions or observations, and neither does the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And no more witnesses either. The next witness has been scheduled for Monday afternoon; is that right, Mr. Withopf? You have everything in your hands and are in charge of producing witnesses, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Right, Mr. President, Your Honours. We have two witnesses for Monday next week and two witnesses for Tuesday next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That being the case, the Trial Chamber takes note that there are no witnesses for Friday, and so we won't be sitting tomorrow afternoon, but we'll reconvene on Monday at quarter past 2.00 to hear the next witnesses and their testimonies. And they will be Prosecution witnesses. So see you all back here on Monday at 2.15. The meeting is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 19th day of January, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.40 p.m.,
